learn.title: Asking for memory
learn.body: `malloc(n)` asks the heap for `n` bytes. It returns the address of the block, as a pointer you can store in any pointer type. If there is no memory to give, it returns `NULL`. It lives in `stdlib.h`.

learn.title: An array of five ints
learn.body: This prints 30, the sum 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 + 16. We ask for room for 5 ints, check for `NULL`, then use the block like an array.

learn.title: Counting the bytes
learn.body: How many bytes does `malloc(5 * sizeof(int))` request?
steps: Always multiply by `sizeof` rather than typing 20

learn.title: Fresh memory is not cleared
learn.body: A new block holds whatever bytes were there before. Reading it before writing gives unpredictable values. If you want zeroes, use `calloc(count, size)` or write the values yourself first.
Write `malloc(n * sizeof *a)` instead of repeating the type. If the type of `a` changes, the size stays right.

questions.prompt: What does `malloc` return when it fails?
questions.explanation: On failure it returns a null pointer, so always test it.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does `malloc(5 * sizeof(int))` request here?
questions.explanation: 5 ints of 4 bytes each is 20 bytes.

questions.prompt: What does a fresh `malloc` block contain?
questions.explanation: It is not cleared. Write before you read.

questions.prompt: What does the example program print?
To get zeroed memory, you can use \_\_ instead of `malloc`.
questions.explanation: `calloc(count, size)` zeroes the block it returns.
